summary: A country on the Apennine Peninsula in southern Europe, the birthplace of the ancient Roman Empire and the Renaissance. Vatican City lies within the capital, Rome, and Italy has one of the largest numbers of World Heritage Sites in the world.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: Rome is the center of Catholicism, with the Holy See located in Vatican City inside Rome, and Italian culture, festivals and town life are deeply shaped by Catholicism. The 1929 Lateran Treaty established Catholicism as the state religion, and schools offered Catholic religion classes. Although its state-religion status was abolished in 1984 and most Italians are still baptized Catholics, the share who attend Mass weekly has fallen to under about 20 percent.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: The postwar economic miracle brought urbanization and wider education, and the referendums legalizing divorce and abortion in the 1970s and 1980s (1974, 1981) showed society's values moving away from the Church. In recent years the fastest growth in the non-religious is in large northern cities and among the younger generation, and the Church's sexual abuse scandals have also accelerated the trend of leaving the Church.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: Italy's Muslims are almost all from immigration in recent decades; from the 1980s, Moroccans, Albanians, Tunisians, Egyptians, Bangladeshis and Pakistanis came to Italy to work. They are mostly concentrated in northern industrial cities such as Milan, Turin and Bologna, but Islam has not yet signed a formal agreement with the government, and the number of official mosques is very small.

ranking.name: Other Christian (Orthodox, Protestant, etc.)
ranking.description: Orthodox believers are mostly immigrants from Romania, Ukraine and Moldova who arrived after the 2000s, and Romanians are Italy's largest foreign community. Protestants include the long-established Waldensians, a reform movement that arose in the 12th century, long persecuted in the Piedmont valleys and granted civil rights only in 1848, as well as Pentecostals introduced in modern times.

religion.background: Christianity reached Rome in the 1st century, and after persecution, Emperor Constantine issued the Edict of Milan in 313 granting it legal status; in 380 it became the state religion of the Roman Empire. The bishop of Rome developed into the pope, and in the Middle Ages the Papal States ruled central Italy for a thousand years. In 1870 the Kingdom of Italy captured Rome and ended the Papal States, leaving church-state relations strained until 1929, when Mussolini signed the Lateran Treaty with the Holy See, recognizing Vatican City State and making Catholicism the state religion. A new concordat in 1984 abolished state-religion status, and in recent decades secularization and immigration have made the religious makeup more diverse.

language.official: The official language is Italian; in some regions German, French, Slovene and others are also official languages.

ranking.name: Italian
ranking.description: Italian is based on the Florentine Tuscan dialect used by Dante in the 14th century, and after unification in 1861 the government made it the language of schools, the army and administration. The state-run television broadcaster RAI, which began broadcasting in 1954, let the whole nation hear the same standard language every day, making Italian the common language of almost everyone, although many people still also use regional languages such as Neapolitan and Sicilian.

ranking.name: German
ranking.description: German is concentrated in South Tyrol (Alto Adige) in the north, which belonged to Austria-Hungary and was ceded to Italy in 1919 after the First World War. Italianization was forcibly pursued under Mussolini, and after the second autonomy statute of 1972 German and Italian enjoy equal official status there, with schools teaching in separate languages.

ranking.name: Romanian
ranking.description: After Romania joined the EU in 2007, large numbers of Romanians went to Italy to work in construction, caregiving and agriculture, and Romanians became Italy's largest foreign community. Romanian is also a Romance language and is close to Italian, so it is relatively easy for immigrants to learn Italian.

language.history: Italian derives from Latin, and after the fall of the Roman Empire very different dialects developed in different places. In the 14th century Dante wrote the Divine Comedy in the Tuscan dialect, and Petrarch and Boccaccio also wrote in it, so Tuscan became the standard of the literary language. At unification in 1861, it is estimated that only about 2.5 to 10 percent of people could speak standard Italian, and most spoke local dialects. Compulsory education after unification, internal migration after the Second World War, and television and radio broadcasting from the 1950s spread standard Italian across the country, but dialects are still used at home today.

ranking.name: Neapolitan pizza
ranking.description: A thin hand-kneaded dough is baked for 60–90 seconds in a wood-fired oven at about 450 degrees Celsius, with a puffed rim and soft center; the classic flavor is Margherita.
ranking.history: Foods topping flatbreads have existed since ancient times, but tomatoes reached Italy from the Americas only in the 16th century, and in the 18th century the poor of Naples began selling flatbreads topped with tomato, forming modern pizza. Legend has it that in 1889 the cook Raffaele Esposito made a pizza in red (tomato), white (mozzarella) and green (basil), the colors of the Italian flag, for the visiting Queen Margherita and named it "Margherita" (the truth of this story is disputed). From the late 19th to the early 20th century Italian immigrants brought pizza to the United States, and after the Second World War it swept the world; in 2017 the art of Neapolitan pizza making was inscribed on UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list.

ranking.name: Spaghetti alla carbonara
ranking.description: Pasta tossed with egg yolks, Pecorino sheep's milk cheese, cured pork cheek (guanciale) and black pepper, with no cream.
ranking.history: Carbonara is a Roman dish, and its earliest documents appear in the early 1950s, so its history is not long. One account says that at the end of the Second World War American troops stationed in Italy brought powdered eggs and bacon, and Roman cooks made this pasta from them; another says it originated in the cooking of the charcoal burners (carbonari) of the Apennine mountains, the name meaning "charcoal burner's style". Together with cacio e pepe and amatriciana it is counted among Rome's classic pasta dishes, and Italians are very firm that it "must not contain cream".

ranking.name: Lasagne
ranking.description: Wide sheets of pasta are layered with meat ragù, béchamel and cheese and baked, the best known being the Bolognese style of the Emilia-Romagna region.
ranking.history: The name lasagne can be traced back to the ancient Greek laganon and the Latin lasanum, and a 14th-century medieval Neapolitan recipe already records a dish layering pasta sheets and cheese. After tomatoes arrived, the south developed versions with tomato sauce, while Bologna in the north is represented by layers of meat sauce and béchamel. In Italy it is often a Sunday family lunch and a festive dish at Carnival, and needs a long time to prepare.

ranking.name: Risotto
ranking.description: Short-grain, high-starch rice (such as Arborio and Carnaroli) is slowly stirred and cooked with broth, and finished with butter and Parmesan cheese, giving a creamy, thick consistency.
ranking.history: Rice probably reached Sicily and Spain via the Arabs in the Middle Ages, and from the 15th century large-scale rice growing began on the Po plain in northern Italy; Lombardy and Piedmont are still Europe's largest rice-producing regions. Risotto therefore became a specialty of northern Italy, in contrast to the pasta-centered south. The most famous, Milanese saffron risotto, is said to originate in a 16th-century story of Milan Cathedral glassworkers coloring with saffron.
ranking.imageCredit: Luca Nebuloni from Milan, Italy・CC BY 2.0・Wikimedia Commons

ranking.name: Tiramisu
ranking.description: Ladyfinger biscuits are soaked in espresso and layered with a cream of mascarpone cheese, egg yolks and sugar, and the surface is dusted with cocoa powder.
ranking.history: Tiramisu is a very young dessert, generally thought to have been born in the 1960s–70s in Treviso in the northeastern region of Veneto, where the restaurant Le Beccherie is often considered its birthplace, although Friuli also has a competing claim. The name means "pick me up" in Venetian dialect, referring to the energy given by coffee and sugar. In the 1980s it spread around the world and became one of the most popular Italian desserts.
